title: Iterator Pattern
summary: Traversing a collection uniformly — array, tree, or graph — without exposing how it's actually built underneath.

slides.markdown:
**Iterator** gives every collection the same simple traversal contract — `hasNext()`/`next()` — regardless of whether it's an array, a linked list, a tree, or a graph underneath. Code that walks the collection never needs to know how it's actually stored.

You already use this every time you write a `for...of` loop or a Python `for x in collection` — the language is calling an Iterator behind the scenes so you never have to think about array indices vs tree traversal vs hash-bucket order.

slides.sectionTitle: The problem: traversing a collection without exposing its internal structure
slides.markdown:
A `BinaryTree` class could expose its traversal by handing out its raw `root` node and letting callers walk `left`/`right` pointers themselves. That works, but now every piece of client code that wants "all the values in order" has to reimplement in-order traversal, and it's directly coupled to the tree's internal node structure — change the tree to a different underlying structure (say, a balanced tree with different node fields) and every caller's traversal code breaks.

The same problem exists for any collection type: a caller shouldn't need to know whether it's array-backed, node-based, or something else just to loop over the elements.

The underlying problem: traversal logic and internal structure are different concerns, but exposing the structure directly forces every caller to reimplement and depend on traversal details that should be the collection's job, not theirs.

slides.sectionTitle: Iterator: a uniform hasNext()/next() contract over any collection
slides.markdown:
**Iterator** defines a small interface — typically `hasNext(): boolean` and `next(): T` — and the collection provides an object implementing it, hiding exactly how traversal actually happens internally. A caller writes the same loop shape — `while (it.hasNext()) { const x = it.next(); ... }` — whether the underlying collection is an array, a tree, or a graph.

The collection decides how its own iterator walks its internal structure (array index, tree recursion, graph BFS/DFS) once, in one place, and every caller reuses that logic through the same two-method interface instead of reinventing it.

This also means multiple independent iterators can traverse the same collection simultaneously, each tracking its own position, without interfering with each other.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: an iterator tracking traversal position separately from the collection
slides.markdown:
The collection itself holds no notion of "where you currently are" in a traversal — that position lives entirely inside the iterator object. This is what lets two iterators walk the same tree at the same time without stepping on each other.

![A Collection with two independent Iterator objects, each holding a current position pointer into a different node](assets/iterator-positions.svg)

Each `next()` call advances only that iterator's own internal position — the collection's data is read, never mutated, by the act of iterating.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: implementing a custom iterator over a tree structure
Compare: external vs internal iterators — for-each vs callback-based
slides.markdown:
| | External iterator | Internal iterator |
|---|---|---|
| Who drives the loop | The caller — explicit `while (it.hasNext())` | The collection — you pass a callback, it calls you |
| Example | Java `Iterator`, a manual `hasNext()`/`next()` loop | `array.forEach(callback)`, `array.map(fn)` |
| Control flow | Caller can pause, break early, or interleave with other logic mid-traversal | Usually can't easily break early or pause without extra signaling |
| Multiple collections at once | Easy — hold two iterators, advance them independently | Awkward — each callback only sees one collection's elements |

**How to decide:** internal iterators (`forEach`/`map`) are more concise for simple "do this to every element" cases; external iterators win when you need to pause, break early, or walk two collections in lockstep.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: mutating a collection while iterating over it
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I can safely add or remove elements from a list while looping over it with `for...of` or an iterator."

**Why it's wrong:** most iterators assume the collection's structure stays stable during traversal. Removing an element while an array-backed iterator holds a numeric index shifts every subsequent element down by one, so the iterator silently skips the element that slid into the just-vacated slot. Many languages go further and raise a `ConcurrentModificationException` (Java) or similarly fail loudly, precisely because silent skipping is worse than crashing.

**Correct model:** either collect the items to remove into a separate list and apply the removals after the loop finishes, or use an iterator explicitly designed for safe removal (Java's `Iterator.remove()`, which updates the iterator's own bookkeeping atomically with the removal).

slides.sectionTitle: Where this shows up: language-level for-each, generators and lazy sequences
slides.markdown:
Virtually every modern language bakes Iterator into a core language feature: Python's `for x in collection` calls `__iter__`/`__next__` under the hood; JavaScript's `for...of` uses the iterable protocol (`Symbol.iterator`); Java's enhanced for-loop compiles to `Iterator` calls. You've been using this pattern constantly without naming it.

**Generators** (Python `yield`, JavaScript generator functions) are Iterator taken further: instead of hand-writing a class with `hasNext()`/`next()`, you write a function that pauses and resumes, and the language builds the iterator object for you — which is also how **lazy/infinite sequences** work (an infinite stream of numbers is fine as long as nothing ever calls `next()` on all of it at once).
